summary: Dioctyl sodium sulfosuccinate (docusate sodium) is an emollient laxative (stool softener) used for the short-term relief and prevention of constipation, especially where straining should be avoided (e.g. after surgery, myocardial infarction, childbirth, or with painful anorectal conditions/hemorrhoids). As a surfactant, it allows water and fat to penetrate and soften the stool, making it easier to pass; it does not directly stimulate peristalsis. It generally produces a soft stool in 1-3 days. It is for short-term use; laxatives should not be used for more than about a week without medical advice, and it should not be used if there is abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or signs of bowel obstruction. It can enhance the absorption of mineral oil (avoid co-administration). Adequate fluid intake supports its action.
indications: Short-term relief of occasional constipation (softening of hard, dry stools)
Prevention of constipation/straining where it is undesirable (e.g. after myocardial infarction or rectal surgery, in hemorrhoids/anal fissure, postpartum)

moa: Docusate is an anionic surfactant (wetting/emollient agent). It lowers the surface tension at the interface between the watery and fatty components of the intestinal contents, allowing water and lipids to penetrate the dry, hardened fecal mass. This hydrates and softens the stool and facilitates easier, less strained passage. It acts as a detergent-like stool softener rather than a stimulant: it does not directly increase intestinal peristalsis. Some increase in intestinal secretion of water and electrolytes may also contribute. Its action is local within the gut; systemic absorption is minimal.

absolute: Acute abdomen / signs of intestinal obstruction, ileus, or undiagnosed abdominal pain, nausea, or vomiting

preg: Docusate is minimally absorbed and is generally considered acceptable for use in pregnancy when a stool softener is needed; use as directed and avoid prolonged use. Maintaining fluid and fiber intake is recommended alongside.
lact: Docusate is poorly absorbed systemically and is considered compatible with breastfeeding; little or no drug is expected to reach the infant through milk.
renal: No dose adjustment is required for renal impairment; docusate acts locally in the gut and is minimally absorbed.
hepatic: No dose adjustment is required for hepatic impairment from docusate itself. Avoid concurrent mineral oil, as docusate enhances absorption of mineral oil which can be problematic.

moderate: Mineral oil - docusate increases its systemic absorption; avoid concomitant use (risk of mineral-oil deposition/granulomas)
Other drugs - by acting as a surfactant docusate may theoretically increase absorption of some co-administered drugs (e.g. has been described with phenolphthalein, certain others)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; adequate fluid intake supports its effect.

emergency: Severe persistent abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, or failure to have a bowel movement (possible obstruction)

Duration of use (limit to about 1 week without medical advice)

pearls: Stool SOFTENER (surfactant) - softens stool but does not stimulate peristalsis; best for preventing straining (post-MI, post-surgery, hemorrhoids, postpartum)
Effect takes 1-3 days; not for rapid relief of acute constipation
Do NOT combine with mineral oil - docusate increases mineral-oil absorption
Considered acceptable in pregnancy and lactation (minimal absorption)
Short-term use only - persistent constipation needs evaluation; avoid laxative dependence

missed: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip the missed dose. Do not take a double dose. Since it is used for symptom relief, you may simply resume when needed.
overdose: Overdose may cause abdominal cramping and diarrhea, which can lead to fluid and electrolyte loss with excessive amounts. There is no specific antidote. Management is supportive - maintain hydration and replace electrolytes if significant diarrhea occurs. Discontinue the laxative.
